analysis.one_liner: Reforms farm subsidies, repeals sugar price supports and tariffs, replaces dairy price supports, and tightens SNAP eligibility.
analysis.headline: The farm subsidy reform bill, introduced with zero cosponsors, was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never received a markup, hearing, or vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the farm safety net: repealing the direct and counter-cyclical payments that flow to commodity producers regardless of need, replacing them with revenue-based payments tied to actual losses, and expanding federally subsidized crop and whole-farm revenue insurance. It would have repealed the sugar program outright — ending loans, marketing quotas, and the tariffs that keep U.S. sugar prices well above world levels — and replaced dairy price supports with a margin protection program. It also extended dozens of nutrition, conservation, and rural energy programs, while tightening SNAP by limiting categorical eligibility and repealing employment and training funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers. Ending the sugar program's loans, quotas, and tariffs would have exposed domestic sugar processors to import competition and likely lowered retail sugar prices, which currently run well above world prices — a cost passed to every household and to food manufacturers. Repealing direct payments — which go to commodity producers regardless of need, and often to large operations and absentee landowners — would have removed a guaranteed taxpayer outlay. Dairy farmers, especially smaller ones, would have gained a margin protection program paying them when milk prices fall below feed costs, with coverage reaching down to small operations through a tiered administrative fee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, taxpayers, and small dairy farms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the direct and counter-cyclical payment programs for covered commodities and peanuts beginning with the 2013 crop year, replacing guaranteed payments with revenue-based ARRM payments that pay only when district and farm revenue fall below a 90% guarantee.

Repeals the sugar loan program, terminates sugar marketing quotas and allotments, and eliminates tariffs on raw cane sugar, beet sugar, and certain refined sugar — ending the price supports and import barriers that keep domestic sugar prices above world levels.

Creates a dairy producer margin protection program that pays farmers when milk prices minus feed costs fall below $4.00 per hundredweight, with administrative fees tiered by size ($100 for operations under 10 million pounds of milk) so small dairies pay the least, and repeals the dairy price support, milk income loss contract, and dairy export subsidy programs.

Requires USDA to offer a whole farm insurance plan paying producers whose gross farm revenue falls below 80% of average, and to offer supplemental area-based coverage for losses not covered by individual policies.
Extends the fresh fruits and vegetables for schools program, senior farmers' market nutrition, emergency food infrastructure grants, and dozens of conservation and rural energy programs.

analysis.who_pays: Some low-income households would lose food assistance: the bill limits SNAP categorical eligibility (the rule letting families enrolled in other assistance programs automatically qualify for food stamps) and repeals funding for SNAP employment and training programs and state performance bonuses. Sugar growers and processors would lose loan support, marketing quotas, and tariff protection, and would face competition from lower-priced imports. Commodity producers would lose guaranteed direct payments and take on more exposure to revenue swings, and dairy producers participating in the new program would have payments withheld when margins are low.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar growers and some SNAP households

drawbacks.text: The bill limits SNAP categorical eligibility and repeals employment and training funding and state bonus payments, which would reduce food assistance for some low-income households even as it extends other nutrition programs.

Eliminating direct payments and sugar tariffs would expose farmers to more revenue risk and domestic sugar processors to import competition, with a transition period in which the old supports are gone but the new ARRM and margin programs have not yet been tested.

The dairy market stabilization program would have handlers withhold a percentage of payments to farmers when margins fall, and remit that money to a board that purchases dairy products and promotes demand — a mechanism critics of similar proposals called government-managed supply control that can raise consumer milk prices.
Basic and supplemental dairy margin payments are expressly exempt from any payment limitation, meaning the largest dairy operations face no cap on program receipts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The subsidy reforms — repealing sugar supports, ending uncapped direct payments, means-testing program access through revenue triggers — would transfer costs from taxpayers and consumers to a small set of protected producers, a real public gain. The offsetting cost is real too: the SNAP eligibility restriction would cut food aid for some working-poor families, and the crop and dairy insurance expansions channel new federal premium subsidies through private insurance companies. On balance the bill is a genuine structural reform of farm programs, weakened by a nutrition restriction and by insurance provisions that entrench the private crop-insurance industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and never received a markup, hearing, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-IN) introduced the REFRESH Act on October 5, 2011, as a reform and reauthorization of agricultural programs.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Agriculture and, in addition, to the Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in either party.
The action history shows no further activity after the initial referral: no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 112th Congress.

Among the provisions that never advanced: repeal of direct and counter-cyclical payments in favor of revenue-based ARRM payments, repeal of the sugar loan program and elimination of sugar tariffs, replacement of dairy price supports with a margin protection program, and limits on SNAP categorical eligibility.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The producers and processors the existing programs protect came out ahead: sugar growers kept their loan program, quotas, and tariffs, commodity producers kept their guaranteed direct payments, and dairy price supports and the subsidized crop insurance industry were left untouched — while consumers and taxpayers continued paying the higher sugar prices and subsidy costs the bill would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar processors, commodity producers, and crop insurers

for.name: Rep. Marlin A. Stutzman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the REFRESH Act on October 5, 2011, proposing repeal of direct payments, the sugar program, and dairy price supports alongside tightened SNAP eligibility.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Chair Frank Lucas)
against.role: Primary committee of referral for farm programs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; the only action after introduction was the referral itself.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means (Chair Dave Camp)
against.role: Second committee of referral, with jurisdiction over the bill's tariff provisions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled consideration of the bill's tariff and revenue provisions; no action is recorded beyond the referral.

against.name: Sugar industry groups
against.role: Producers and processors protected by the sugar loan program, quotas, and tariffs
against.what_they_did: Defended the existing sugar program during the farm bill debate, in which proposals to curtail sugar supports were pushed aside.

sides.party_line_note: No member of either party cosponsored the bill, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition shows up in the record; the bill simply stalled without recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill repeals the sugar loan program, marketing quotas, and tariffs on cane, beet, and refined sugar that keep U.S. sugar prices well above world levels. Ending those protections would lower costs for consumers and food manufacturers at the expense of the protected growers and processors.

The bill expands the federal crop insurance system — new supplemental area coverage, whole-farm revenue plans, and a wider adjusted gross revenue pilot — with the Commodity Credit Corporation covering a set share of premiums and a 6% reimbursement rate for insurers on supplemental coverage. Farmers gain new tools, but the delivery of the safety net stays locked through private insurance companies at taxpayer expense.

They lose the guaranteed direct and counter-cyclical payments — historically flowing to large operations and often to landowners who don't farm — and gain revenue-based ARRM payments and expanded insurance that pay only on actual losses. Taxpayers stop funding payments unrelated to need.

Price supports, the milk income loss contract, and export subsidies are repealed in favor of a margin protection program that pays when milk prices minus feed costs fall below thresholds, with fees scaled so small farms pay least. But payments are exempt from limitations, and the stabilization program withholds a share of farmers' milk checks when margins are low — a supply-control mechanism that can raise consumer prices.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals)
industries.note: Eliminating sugar tariffs and import quotas would let manufacturers buy sugar at world prices, lowering input costs that are currently passed to consumers.
The bill extends the Rural Energy for America, biomass crop assistance, and rural energy savings programs while eliminating the feedstock flexibility program for bioenergy producers.
